At a glance

Best months
March and April for the Castro Verde bustard leks and the spring steppe, late September into the first week of October for the Sagres raptor passage, and late May to early August for the Madeira and Azores pelagics
Getting around
A hire car on the mainland. Lisbon, Porto and Faro carry the full desks, and the country is small enough to cross in a day
The one thing to know
Castro Verde is a working farmed steppe rather than a reserve, so the birds are on private land seen from public tracks. The Liga para a Protecao da Natureza programme is what keeps the farming compatible with the bustards

Where: The Graciosa islets, Azores

When: Late April to July

When to Go

The Portuguese year runs on two things: the steppe, which is at its best before the summer burns it, and Sagres, which happens in one fortnight in autumn. The islands run to their own calendar entirely, because the pelagic season is short.

spring

March to May

The season most itineraries run. Bustards display through March and early April before the grass grows tall enough to hide them, and the whole country is singing.

Go for Steppe leks run, raptors breed on the border cliffs, and spring passage crosses the estuaries.

Trade off Easter lifts prices, and the good Alentejo guesthouses fill their April dates early.

Typical daily average
  • Porto: 9 to 18 °C / 48 to 64 °F
  • Lisboa: 11 to 19 °C / 52 to 66 °F
  • Faro: 11 to 21 °C / 52 to 70 °F

summer

June to August

The mainland interior runs hot and the steppe empties after the harvest. This is the island season: the Madeira and Azores pelagics are at their peak.

Go for Zino's Petrel, Monteiro's Storm-petrel and the shearwater colonies.

Trade off Over forty degrees in the Alentejo and Guadiana in high summer. Birding is early morning work.

Typical daily average
  • Porto: 15 to 24 °C / 59 to 75 °F
  • Lisboa: 17 to 27 °C / 63 to 81 °F
  • Faro: 18 to 28 °C / 64 to 82 °F

autumn

September to October

Sagres. Raptors funnel into the southwest corner and pile up waiting for the wind, and the seabird passage runs off the cape at the same time.

Go for The raptor crossing, the seabirds moving offshore, and wader passage through the Algarve and the estuaries.

Trade off The festival week books out. Reserve accommodation in Sagres and Vila do Bispo well ahead.

Typical daily average
  • Porto: 12 to 22 °C / 54 to 72 °F
  • Lisboa: 16 to 24 °C / 61 to 75 °F
  • Faro: 16 to 25 °C / 61 to 77 °F

winter

November to February

Mild, wet in the north, and the estuaries hold their largest wader numbers of the year. The steppe keeps its resident specialities.

Go for Wintering waders and wildfowl, flamingos in the Algarve, Black-winged Kite and the resident eagles.

Trade off Snow closes the top of Serra da Estrela and the northern sierras are genuinely wet.

Typical daily average
  • Porto: 6 to 15 °C / 43 to 59 °F
  • Lisboa: 9 to 16 °C / 48 to 61 °F
  • Faro: 9 to 18 °C / 48 to 64 °F

Where to Bird

Colours match each region. Select a marker to open its entry below.

One pin per region, and the parks and stops inside each region card carry their own coordinates. The mainland regions run down the Atlantic coast, and Madeira and the Azores sit far out to the southwest and west, drawn where they actually are rather than boxed into a corner.

Itineraries

  1. Lisbon (LIS)in
  2. 1Alcochete

1 day

A Lisbon Layover

Lisbon (LIS), the Tagus estuary, Lisbon

EVOA's hides are forty minutes from the terminal and the tide table decides the day. A rising tide pushes the waders in close.

  1. Faro (FAO)in

4 days

Castro Verde in Spring

Faro (FAO), Castro Verde, Mertola

Fly to Faro, drive ninety minutes north onto the plains and base at Castro Verde. Bustards at dawn, then the Guadiana scarps for Bonelli's Eagle and Black Stork.

  1. Faro (FAO)in
  2. 1Vila do Bispo

6 days

The Sagres Raptor Passage

Faro (FAO), Ria Formosa, Sagres, Cape St Vincent

The last week of September into the first week of October. Cabranosa in the morning for the raptor build-up, the cape for seabird passage, and the Algarve wetlands when the wind is wrong.

  1. Funchal (FNC)in
  2. 1Pico do Areeiro
  3. 2Ponta de São Lourenço

6 days

Madeira and the Laurisilva

Funchal (FNC), Ribeiro Frio 2 nights, Pico do Areeiro 1 night, Ponta de São Lourenço 1 night, a pelagic day, Funchal (FNC) out

A separate flight and a separate bird list. The laurel forest at Ribeiro Frio is older than the last ice age, a petrel breeds on the Areeiro ledges above it, and the pelagic out of Funchal reaches the Desertas seabirds.

  1. Porto (OPO)in
  2. 1Miranda do Douro
  3. 2Manteigas
  4. 3Salvaterra do Extremo

9 days

The Border Canyons

Porto (OPO), the Douro Internacional, Serra da Estrela, Tejo Internacional

North to south down the Spanish frontier. It takes the two raptor canyons with the mountains between them, and the Douro river boat is worth the morning.

  1. Porto (OPO)in
  2. 1Miranda do Douro
  3. 2Manteigas
  4. 3Salvaterra do Extremo
  5. 4Alcochete

14 days

Portugal End to End

Porto (OPO), Peneda-Geres, the Douro Internacional, Serra da Estrela, Tejo Internacional, the Tagus, Castro Verde, the Algarve, Faro

Land in the north and fly home from Faro, and work down the country as you go. Spring covers the most of it, with the steppe still green and the mountains open.

The Algarve wetlands

A barrier island lagoon running sixty kilometres behind Faro, with working salt pans at either end of it

Greater Flamingo, Spoonbill, Caspian Tern and Audouin's Gull are on the water most of the year, and the working salt pans at Castro Marim and Tavira concentrate them. A first Portuguese trip usually starts here because the sites sit close together.

  • When: Good all year. Purple Swamphen, Greater Flamingo and Eurasian Spoonbill hold the ground through the year.
  • Getting there: Faro takes the flights and the whole of the best birding sits inside an area about 150 by 200 kilometres. The Algarve itself can be worked on public transport, and the Alentejo needs a vehicle. Roads are poor and the accident rate is the worst in Europe, so the driving wants attention.
  • Look for: Purple Swamphen, Greater Flamingo, Eurasian Spoonbill, Caspian Tern, Audouin's Gull, Kentish Plover, Black-winged Stilt
  • Parks and reserves: Parque Natural da Ria Formosa (natural park)
  • Stops:
    • : A barrier-island lagoon running sixty kilometres behind the eastern Algarve coast, and the European stronghold of the Purple Swamphen.
    • : A golf resort with a public boardwalk and hide over the Ludo saltpans. It gives the easiest Purple Swamphen in Portugal.
    • : The farm track between the saltpans and the lagoon behind Faro airport. Walk it for waders, Little Bittern and Red-crested Pochard.
    • : Saltmarsh and working saltpans on the Guadiana at the Spanish border. Greater Flamingo, Caspian Tern and Spoonbill use them.
    • : A coastal lagoon behind the dunes near Albufeira, with a boardwalk. It gives the best chance of Glossy Ibis and Marbled Teal in the west Algarve.
    • : Working pans east of Tavira, along the causeway. They fill with roosting waders as the lagoon covers.
  • Also covers: Castro Marim salt pans, Ludo, Parque Natural da Ria Formosa, Quinta do Lago, Ria Formosa Natural Park, Salgados lagoon, Tavira salt pans, Tavira saltpans
  • Also watch for: Bottlenose Dolphin works the Ria Formosa channels and the boats out of Faro find them most days. European Chameleon holds the coastal pine and dune between Faro and Tavira, the only chameleon in Europe.

Castro Verde and the Alentejo steppes

Cereal steppe farmed the old way under a conservation programme, holding most of the country's bustards in a few thousand hectares

The one region every operator sells, and the heart of the Alentejo. Castro Verde holds Great Bustard, Little Bustard, Montagu's Harrier, Black-bellied Sandgrouse and Lesser Kestrel in the same few thousand hectares under a Liga para a Proteção da Natureza programme, and over ninety-five per cent of Portugal's Little Bustards are on these plains.

  • Habitat: Open grassland runs east of Almodovar and Castro Verde and carries the bustards and the other steppe birds. White Stork nests sit on the telegraph poles, and Spanish Sparrow squats in the base of them. The medieval hilltop town of Mertola above the Guadiana holds the largest Lesser Kestrel colony in the country.
  • When: February to July, while Lesser Kestrel is in. Great Bustard, Little Bustard and Black-bellied Sandgrouse are on site in all twelve months. Montagu's Harrier is away from October to February.
  • Getting there: Either take the N267 to Mertola, or head north from Albufeira on the longer but faster route through Ourique, then east to Castro Verde and on to Mertola, which runs one to two hours. Almost any promising grassland along the way is worth stopping for, and the tracks off the N123 two or three kilometres east of Castro Verde have been the most productive.
  • Look for: Great Bustard, Little Bustard, Montagu's Harrier, Black-bellied Sandgrouse, Lesser Kestrel, Calandra Lark, Eurasian Stone-curlew, Iberian Grey Shrike
  • Parks and reserves: Zona de Protecção Especial de Castro Verde (special protection area)
  • Stops:
    • : The Liga para a Protecao da Natureza field centre on the steppe, with a hide. Ask here where the bustards are displaying this week.
    • : A village on the northern edge of the reserve. The quiet farm roads that hold Great Bustard and Little Bustard start here.
    • : Open cereal and fallow west of the main road. Drive it slowly for sandgrouse coming to drink.
    • : Rolling dry pasture on the reserve's eastern side, and reliable ground for Montagu's Harrier and Lesser Kestrel.
    • : A village south of the reserve, with a road running out onto the plain. It is the local site for Black-bellied Sandgrouse.
  • Also covers: Casével, Entradas, Guerreiros, Penedo Gordo, Santa Bárbara de Padrões, Vale Gonçalinho Environmental Education Centre, Zona de Protecção Especial de Castro Verde
  • Also watch for: Iberian Hare is the mammal of the open plains and Egyptian Mongoose crosses the tracks in daylight. Ocellated Lizard, the largest lizard in Europe, uses the dry stone walls.

Sagres and Cape St Vincent

The southwest corner of Europe, where autumn raptors stack up on the headland waiting for a wind to cross on

The southwest corner of Europe, and the funnel every soaring bird uses in autumn. Raptors pile up at Cabranosa and Vila do Bispo waiting for the wind, and the seabird passage off Cape St Vincent runs at the same time. The festival in the first week of October exists because of it.

  • Habitat: Cabo de Sao Vicente is the southwestern extremity of Europe, where the limestone cliffs stand 150 metres high, with dry heathland running inland behind them.
  • When: August to November, while Egyptian Vulture and Short-toed Snake Eagle are on site. Great Skua holds the ground through the year. European Honey Buzzard is here from August to October. Booted Eagle is here from September to December.
  • Getting there: The pelagic species are far more likely on the boat trips out of Sagres or Portimao in late summer and early autumn than from the headlands.
  • Look for: Booted Eagle, Short-toed Snake Eagle, European Honey Buzzard, Egyptian Vulture, Cory's Shearwater, Great Skua, Western Black-eared Wheatear
  • Parks and reserves: Parque Natural do Sudoeste Alentejano e Costa Vicentina (natural park)
  • Stops:
    • : The southwestern corner of Europe, a sheer headland with a lighthouse. Every autumn raptor turns here before crossing.
    • : The walled promontory east of the cape. Walk it for Blue Rock Thrush, Alpine Swift and the seabird passage off its point.
    • : A low ridge of scrub inland of the cape, and the staffed raptor watchpoint through the September and October passage.
    • : The small town the whole cape area is reached from, with the coastal plateau and its wheatears around it.
    • : A cork oak and pine wood inland. Woodchat Shrike, Short-toed Treecreeper and the migrant passerines drop in here.
  • Also covers: Barão de São João, Cabranosa, Cape St Vincent, Fortaleza de Sagres, Parque Natural do Sudoeste Alentejano e Costa Vicentina, the Sagres pelagic departure point, Vila do Bispo
  • Also watch for: The same headland watch that produces the raptors produces Common Dolphin and Bottlenose Dolphin offshore, with Sperm Whale on the deeper pelagic runs.

The Tagus and Sado estuaries

Two tidal estuaries either side of Lisbon, one holding the largest wader concentration in the country

Two estuaries either side of Lisbon, both tide-dependent and both enormous. The Tagus holds the largest wader concentration in Portugal, with EVOA's hides giving the reliable close view, and the Sado rice fields and Comporta salt pans carry Black-winged Stilt, Collared Pratincole and a resident bottlenose dolphin population.

  • Habitat: The Tejo reserve covers 145 square kilometres of salina and marsh, with cork-oak woodland to the south of the entrance. On the Sado, 230 square kilometres of the south side lies inside a reserve.
  • When: March to September. Pied Avocet, Black-tailed Godwit and Dunlin are on site in all twelve months. Collared Pratincole is here from March to August. Little Tern is here from April to September.
  • Getting there: For the Tejo reserve turn south at Porto Alto on the N10 east of Vila Franca de Xira onto the N118, then west after 10 km onto a track that reaches the gate after 4 km, and walk the last 1.5 km to the salinas. The north side of the Sado is reached by road through Alcacer do Sal and by the vehicle ferry from Troia to Setubal.
  • Look for: Collared Pratincole, Pied Avocet, Black-tailed Godwit, Dunlin, Glossy Ibis, Little Tern, Common Redshank
  • Parks and reserves: Reserva Natural do Estuário do Tejo (nature reserve), Reserva Natural do Estuário do Sado (nature reserve)
  • Stops:
    • : Working and abandoned pans on the estuary's south shore, twenty minutes from Lisbon. Greater Flamingo, Avocet and Black-winged Stilt use them.
    • : A track out across the reclaimed marsh on the north shore, and the estuary's best ground for Little Bustard and Collared Pratincole.
    • : Saltpans beside the Vasco da Gama bridge. Watch from the road as the wader roost forms on a high tide.
    • : Rice fields and pine behind the Sado's northern dunes. Purple Heron, Glossy Ibis and Black-winged Kite hold them.
    • : A stilt-built fishing harbour on the Sado. The mudflats below it hold waders and the estuary's Osprey.
  • Also covers: Alcochete salt pans, Alcochete saltpans, Carrasqueira, Comporta, EVOA visitor centre, Ponta da Erva, Reserva Natural do Estuário do Sado, Reserva Natural do Estuário do Tejo, Samouco
  • Also watch for: The Sado holds a resident Bottlenose Dolphin population of around thirty animals, one of very few resident groups in Europe. Setúbal is where it is watched from.

The Guadiana valley and Mértola scarps

A schist gorge cut by the Guadiana, birded off the cliff tops above Mértola rather than across open ground

The Guadiana cuts a gorge through the Alentejo schist and the scarps above Mertola hold Bonelli's Eagle, Egyptian Vulture, Black Stork and Blue Rock Thrush. Pulo do Lobo is the set piece. The birding here is cliff work and patience rather than the open sweep of the steppe.

  • When: Good all year. Bonelli's Eagle, Black Stork and Blue Rock Thrush stay through the year.
  • Look for: Bonelli's Eagle, Black Stork, Blue Rock Thrush, Black Wheatear, Great Spotted Cuckoo, Alpine Swift, Eurasian Eagle-Owl
  • Parks and reserves: Parque Natural do Vale do Guadiana (natural park)
  • Stops:
    • : A hill town above the Guadiana with a castle. Its scarps carry Lesser Kestrel, Blue Rock Thrush and Black Stork within sight of the streets.
    • : The river's schist gorge and the dry pasture above it. Bonelli's Eagle, Eagle Owl and Rufous-tailed Rock Thrush hold it.
    • : A waterfall where the Guadiana drops through a narrow schist channel, on a dirt road. Black Stork use the ledges.
    • : An abandoned copper mine and its reservoir. Rock Sparrow and Black Wheatear hold the ruins, with Little Bustard on the ground around.
    • : A village on the plateau north of the gorge, and the way onto the open steppe that holds Great Bustard.
  • Also covers: Alcaria Ruiva, Guadiana Valley Natural Park, Mértola, Mina de São Domingos, Parque Natural do Vale do Guadiana, Pomarão, Pulo do Lobo waterfall
  • Also watch for: Eurasian Otter works the Guadiana and its tributaries, Egyptian Mongoose the schist scrub above, and Ocellated Lizard the warm rock at Pulo do Lobo.

The Douro wine country

A canyon on the Spanish frontier carrying one of the densest raptor cliffs in Iberia, with a river boat below it

The Douro Internacional is a canyon on the Spanish border with one of Iberia's densest raptor cliffs: Griffon Vulture, Egyptian Vulture, Golden Eagle, Bonelli's Eagle and Black Stork all on the same rock faces. Miranda do Douro is the base, and the river boat gives the view the road cannot.

  • When: Good all year. Griffon Vulture, Golden Eagle and Red-billed Chough stay through the year.
  • Look for: Griffon Vulture, Golden Eagle, Red-billed Chough, Rock Bunting, Common Rock Thrush, Eurasian Crag Martin, Ortolan Bunting
  • Parks and reserves: Parque Natural do Douro Internacional (natural park)
  • Stops:
    • : The river's canyon along the Spanish border, granite and schist cliffs two hundred metres deep. Egyptian Vulture, Griffon Vulture and Bonelli's Eagle hold them.
    • : A frontier town on the canyon rim. The boat trips into the gorge leave from below the dam.
    • : A town at the park's southern end, with viewpoints over the canyon and almond groves that hold Woodchat Shrike and Golden Oriole.
    • : The walled hill town of Castelo Rodrigo above the plateau, and the base for the Faia Brava reserve nearby.
    • : The terraced vineyard heart of the Douro downstream. It is worth the drive for the landscape and for Red-rumped Swallow over the river.
  • Also covers: Figueira de Castelo Rodrigo, Freixo de Espada à Cinta, Miranda do Douro, Parque Natural do Douro Internacional, Peso da Régua, Porto
  • Also watch for: Iberian Wolf ranges the plateau above the canyon and is monitored across the Douro Internacional. Eurasian Otter uses the river itself and Spanish Ibex has recolonised the Spanish side.

Tejo Internacional and the eastern frontier

The same frontier canyon further south, and the Portuguese half of a raptor landscape that runs on into Extremadura

Salvaterra do Extremo and Monfortinho put you on the cliffs, and both Black Vulture and Spanish Imperial Eagle use this ground.

  • When: Good all year. Cinereous Vulture and Black-winged Kite are here in every month. Woodchat Shrike is here from March to August.
  • Look for: Cinereous Vulture, Spanish Imperial Eagle, Peregrine Falcon, Black-winged Kite, Woodchat Shrike, European Roller, Western Orphean Warbler
  • Parks and reserves: Parque Natural do Tejo Internacional (natural park)
  • Stops:
    • : The Tagus canyon on the Spanish border, quartzite and schist. Black Vulture, Black Stork and Spanish Imperial Eagle carry it.
    • : A spa village at the park's northern end, with the Erges river gorge below it and the Serra de Penha Garcia behind.
    • : A village on the eastern frontier itself, on the canyon rim with a viewpoint over the Erges. It gives the surest Bonelli's Eagle in the park.
    • : The district town and its reservoir. It is the base for the open dehesa (open oak parkland grazed beneath cork and holm oak) that holds Great Bustard and Montagu's Harrier.
    • : A village at the heart of the park's dehesa. The roads out to the vulture cliffs start from it.
  • Also covers: Idanha-a-Nova, Monfortinho, Parque Natural do Tejo Internacional, Rosmaninhal, Salvaterra do Extremo, Segura, Tejo Internacional Natural Park
  • Also watch for: Eurasian Otter and Egyptian Mongoose both use the river corridor, and Iberian Lynx has been released into the Guadiana basin to the south under the Iberian recovery programme.

Serra da Estrela and the central highlands

Glacial granite topping out at Torre, the only Portuguese ground high enough for the mountain birds

Portugal's central high country, glacial and granite, tops out at Torre. The birds are the mountain set that the lowlands lack: Bluethroat, Water Pipit, Alpine Accentor, Rock Thrush and Red-billed Chough. Snow closes the top in winter, and the season here runs late spring to early autumn.

  • When: Good all year. Rock Sparrow and Dartford Warbler stay through the year. Northern Wheatear is away from November to March.
  • Look for: Bluethroat, Water Pipit, Alpine Accentor, Northern Wheatear, Ring Ouzel, Rock Sparrow, Dartford Warbler
  • Parks and reserves: Parque Natural da Serra da Estrela (natural park)
  • Stops:
    • : The highest point in mainland Portugal at 1,993 m, and a road climbs to it. Water Pipit, Northern Wheatear and Alpine Accentor hold the plateau.
    • : The town in the glacial trough of the Zêzere, and the base for the mountain's walking and its Bluethroat.
    • : A birch grove at the head of the Zêzere valley under the cirque wall, and a sheltered spot for Bluethroat and Dipper.
    • : A scatter of houses on the granite shoulder above Manteigas. It is worth the stop for Rock Bunting, Ortolan Bunting and Red-billed Chough.
  • Also covers: Covão d'Ametade, Manteigas, Parque Natural da Serra da Estrela, Penhas Douradas, Serra da Estrela Natural Park, Torre, Zêzere glacial valley
  • Also watch for: The Serra da Estrela mountain dog still works the flocks here. Wild Boar and Roe Deer use the valley woodland, and Iberian Wolf ranges the wilder edge of the massif.

Peneda-Gerês and the northern sierras

The country's only national park, in the far northern corner on the Galician border, wet Atlantic oak and granite tor

The only national park in Portugal, on the Galician border, and a different country from the Alentejo: oak and pine, granite tors and wet Atlantic weather. Golden Eagle, Short-toed Snake Eagle and Iberian Green Woodpecker, with a wolf population that occasionally shows.

  • When: Good all year. Iberian Green Woodpecker, Common Firecrest and Tawny Pipit are here in every month. Red-backed Shrike is here from May to September.
  • Look for: Iberian Green Woodpecker, Eurasian Wryneck, Common Firecrest, Red-backed Shrike, Whinchat, Tawny Pipit, Grey Wagtail
  • National park: Parque Nacional da Peneda-Gerês
  • Stops:
    • : Old oak forest on the road towards the Spanish border, and the park's best woodland for Middle Spotted Woodpecker and Short-toed Treecreeper.
    • : A village at the head of the Homem valley with a museum and trailheads, and the practical base for the southern park.
    • : A sanctuary under a granite cliff in the park's northern half, with Golden Eagle and Red-billed Chough over it.
    • : A border village whose granary field of stone espigueiros sits under a castle. The reservoir below holds grebes and herons.
    • : The highest village in the park, on open moor at 1,100 m, and the ground for Bluethroat and Whinchat.
  • Also covers: Campo do Gerês, Ermida, Lindoso, Mata de Albergaria, Parque Nacional da Peneda-Gerês, Peneda, Arcos de Valdevez, Pitões das Júnias, Senhora da Peneda
  • Also watch for: Iberian Wolf holds its southernmost Portuguese population in this park. The Garrano, a native hill pony, ranges free on the summit ridges, and Roe Deer and Wild Boar use the oak below.

Madeira and its endemic laurisilva

Laurel forest older than the last ice age, with a petrel breeding on the Areeiro ledges above it

Trocaz Pigeon and Madeira Firecrest are on the forest trails at Ribeiro Frio, and Zino's Petrel breeds on the Pico do Areeiro ledges. The pelagics out of Funchal are a separate product and the real draw.

  • When: Good all year. Trocaz Pigeon, Madeira Firecrest and Plain Swift stay through the year.
  • Look for: Trocaz Pigeon, Madeira Firecrest, Zino's Petrel, Desertas Petrel, Plain Swift, Berthelot's Pipit, Band-rumped Storm Petrel
  • Parks and reserves: Parque Natural da Madeira (natural park)
  • Stops:
    • : A laurel forest reserve on the island's north side, with a levada walk from the road. It is the reliable place for Trocaz Pigeon and Madeira Firecrest.
    • : The third highest peak, and a road climbs to 1,818 m. It is the accessible ground for the Madeira Petrel colonies that nest on the ledges below.
    • : A treeless volcanic peninsula at the island's eastern tip, on a marked path, with Berthelot's Pipit and Plain Swift.
    • : The town on the east coast beside the airport, and the harbour the Desertas and pelagic boats leave from.
    • : The road head at 1,590 m on Madeira's northern spine, and the start of the walk to Pico Ruivo. The petrels cross the high ridge at night.
  • Also covers: Achada do Teixeira, Laurisilva forest of Ribeiro Frio, Machico, Parque Natural da Madeira, Pico do Areeiro, Madeira, Pico Ruivo, Ponta de São Lourenço, the Oceanodroma pelagic departure point
  • Also watch for: Monk Seal has recovered in the Desertas islands from a dozen animals to well over a hundred, and the pelagics out of Funchal find Short-finned Pilot Whale, Bryde's Whale and Atlantic Spotted Dolphin.

The Azores seabird islands

Nine islands two hours further into the Atlantic, carrying a seabird list nowhere else in Europe holds

The Graciosa islets hold Monteiro's Storm-petrel, which breeds nowhere else on earth. Cory's Shearwater is everywhere in summer and the pelagics run out to the offshore banks.

  • When: April to November, while Common Tern is here. Azores Bullfinch, Barolo Shearwater and Yellow-legged Gull stay through the year. Roseate Tern is away from November to March.
  • Look for: Monteiro's Storm Petrel, Azores Bullfinch, Roseate Tern, Great Shearwater, Barolo Shearwater, Common Tern, Yellow-legged Gull
  • Parks and reserves: Ilhéus das Formigas Marine Reserve
  • Stops:
    • : Small offshore islets cleared of rodents. Monteiro's Storm Petrel breeds here and nowhere else in the world.
    • : The central island with the international airport, and the base for the inter-island flights.
    • : The largest island, with crater lakes, laurel forest and the archipelago's main town at Ponta Delgada.
    • : The volcano island. Its channel with Faial is where the whale and seabird boats work.
    • : The island across the channel from Pico, with Horta marina and the Capelinhos volcanic point for seabird passage.
  • Also covers: Faial, Graciosa islets of Praia, Baixo and Baleia, Ilhéus das Formigas Marine Reserve, Pico, São Miguel, Terceira, the Bank of Fortune pelagic grounds
  • Also watch for: The Azores is one of the best whale-watching grounds in the world: Sperm Whale is resident, and Blue Whale, Fin Whale and Sei Whale pass through on northward migration in April and May.

Preparation

BeakBrain Learn the Portuguese list before you travel The steppe birds are a distant shape in heat haze and the seabirds are a silhouette off a moving boat. Every species here as a collector card. Learn these 560 birds before you fly

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the best time to go birding in Portugal?

March and April if you want one answer. Great Bustards are displaying at Castro Verde, the steppe is still green and the border canyons have their raptors on the nest. Late September into early October is the other answer, for the raptor passage at Sagres.

Where do I go for bustards in Portugal?

Castro Verde, in the Alentejo, ninety minutes north of Faro. It is a cereal steppe farmed under an Liga para a Protecao da Natureza conservation programme and it holds both Great and Little Bustard, along with Montagu's Harrier, Black-bellied Sandgrouse and Lesser Kestrel.

Is Sagres worth a trip on its own?

In the first week of October, yes. Raptors funnel into the southwest corner of Europe and wait for the wind to cross, and Cabranosa and Vila do Bispo give the view. The Sagres Birdwatching Festival runs in the same window.

Do I need a car in Portugal?

For the mainland, yes. The steppe tracks, the canyon viewpoints and the estuary hides are all well away from public transport. Lisbon and Faro both have the full hire desks.

Are Madeira and the Azores part of a Portugal birding trip?

They are sold as their own trips rather than folded into a mainland circuit. Both are island and pelagic destinations with their own endemics, and each takes a week of its own.

What certification should I look for in Portuguese accommodation?

Green Key, which the Portuguese call Chave Verde. It runs at real national scale here, with 446 establishments awarded in the 2026 edition and a public register anyone can search.

Which birds is Portugal best for in Europe?

Black-winged Kite is the standout, more reliable here than anywhere else in Europe. Little Bustard is another, with over ninety-five per cent of the national population on the Alentejo plains, and Zino's Petrel breeds nowhere but Madeira.

Who are the birding institutions in Portugal?

SPEA is the BirdLife partner, founded in 1993 with around three thousand two hundred members. Liga para a Protecao da Natureza is the oldest conservation body in the country and runs the Castro Verde programme, and ICNF manages the protected areas.

Can I bird here with limited mobility?

Sites on this page differ from each other more than any rating could carry, so this is the framework the standard British guides use, and the reserve's own page and warden hold the answers.

  • Permission · some reserves open ground to disabled visitors that is closed to everyone else, and it is granted by asking.
  • Priority · parking bays, hides and the nearest paths are often held for disabled visitors. Ask what is reserved and how to claim it.
  • Parking · how close a car reaches the birds shapes the whole day. Ring ahead for the nearest hard standing to the water or the hide.
  • Paths · surfaces, gradients and gate widths vary inside a single reserve. Ask which trail is boarded, surfaced or level.
  • Perches · a hide with a low window, or a bench where the view opens, turns a viewpoint into a morning.

Every reserve above with its own link carries its access detail there, and a warden answers what a page cannot.

Birding Community

SPEA The BirdLife partner, founded in 1993 and the partner since 1999, with around three thousand two hundred members. It runs the rarities committee and the seabird work on the islands. Visit LPN Portugal's oldest conservation body, founded in 1948. It runs the Castro Verde Sustainable Programme, which is why the steppe is still farmed the way the bustards need. Visit ICNF The government body for protected areas and forests, formed in 2012. Every mainland natural park above sits under it. Visit IFCN Madeira Madeira runs its own nature and forest institute, separate from mainland ICNF, and it is the authority for the laurisilva, the evergreen laurel forest kept wet by cloud, and the Zino's Petrel ledges.
